claim: pgvector supports four vector types: vector (4 bytes/dim, up to 16,000 dims), halfvec (2 bytes/dim, up to 16,000 dims), sparsevec (up to 16,000 non-zero elements), and bit (up to 64,000 dims).
quote: vector: Up to 16,000 dimensions, storing 4 bytes per dimension; halfvec: half-precision floats (2 bytes per dimension); sparsevec: Up to 16,000 non-zero elements; bit: Binary vectors up to 64,000 dimensions

claim: The pgvector/pgvector GitHub repository has approximately 21,679 stars as of June 2026.
quote: The `stargazers_count` field value is **21679**.

claim: pgvector 0.7.0 added the halfvec and sparsevec types plus L1 distance, hamming_distance and jaccard_distance functions; indexing limits are ~4,000 dims for halfvec and ~1,000 nonzero dims for sparsevec.
quote: pgvector version 0.7.0 added new vector types, including halfvec (2-byte floats; indexing up to 4,000 dimensions) and sparsevec (indexing up to 1,000 nonzero dimensions)

claim: Embeddings are generated client-side by an embedding model (e.g. OpenAI text-embedding-3-small) then written to a vector column; OpenAI embeddings use 1536 dimensions and a cosine-distance query looks like ORDER BY embedding <=> $1::vector LIMIT 4.
quote: embedding generation happens in the client.embeddings.create() method ... CREATE TABLE documents ( id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, content TEXT, embedding VECTOR(1536) ) ... ORDER BY embedding <=> $1::vector LIMIT 4. The `<=>` operator calculates cosine distance

claim: Workflow: enable the extension (create extension vector), a model generates the embedding array for text, the array is inserted into a vector(n) column, and similarity search uses ORDER BY embedding <-> query LIMIT k, enabling RAG.
quote: A model creates embeddings ... inserted into a Postgres table with a vector column ... SELECT * FROM items WHERE category_id = 123 ORDER BY embedding <-> '[3,1,2]' LIMIT 5; ... valuable for retrieval augmented generation (RAG)

claim: On Supabase benchmarks HNSW showed roughly 3x better performance than IVFFlat on 224k 1536-dim Wikipedia embeddings, and over 6x better on 1M DBpedia vectors at accuracy@10=0.98, outperforming Qdrant on equal compute at 0.99 accuracy; ef_search was tuned 100-250 for accuracy.
quote: HNSW demonstrated 3 times better performance than IVFFlat with superior accuracy ... over six times better performance while maintaining the same level of accuracy at accuracy@10=0.98

claim: Neon recommends HNSW m of 12-48, ef_construction at least twice m, ef_search equal to or larger than the query LIMIT k; for IVFFlat start probes at lists/10 up to 1M rows or sqrt(lists) above, noting recall plateaus with diminishing returns as probes rise.
quote: Should be set to at least twice the value of m ... Higher values increase accuracy (recall), but also increase index size in memory and construction time

claim: The 2,000-dim limit on indexed vector columns blocks indexing of 3,072-dim text-embedding-3-large unless halfvec is used; halfvec (pgvector 0.7.0+) uses 2 bytes per dimension, halving storage and doubling the indexable limit to 4,000 dimensions.
quote: halfvec doubles the HNSW/IVFFlat limit from 2,000 to 4,000 because half the bytes per dimension means twice the capacity

claim: HNSW indexes need to fit in RAM for good performance; at 50M 768-dim vectors this is roughly 150GB+ of memory, and standard pgvector HNSW begins to slow noticeably above 5-10M vectors, where disk-based extensions like pgvectorscale (DiskANN) help.
quote: the HNSW index needs to fit in memory for good performance, and at 50M vectors with 768 dimensions you're looking at roughly 150GB+ of RAM

claim: pgvector 0.8.0 (released 2024-10-30) added iterative index scans as a technique to prevent overfiltering, continuing to search the index until a configurable threshold if the initial scan does not satisfy the query.
quote: iterative index scans, which is a technique to prevent 'overfiltering' or not returning enough results to satisfy the conditions of a query ... pgvector will continue to search the index until it hits a configurable threshold

claim: Pre-0.8 filtering ran after the index scan, so with default HNSW ef_search=40 a 10%-selective filter yielded roughly 4 usable rows; 0.8.0 iterative scans lifted recall on filtered queries from as low as 1-10% to 100% and gave up to 9.4x faster queries (123.3ms to 13.1ms).
quote: With default HNSW settings (ef_search = 40), if only 10% of data matched your filter, you'd retrieve roughly 4 usable results ... Category-filtered queries: 10% to 100% recall ... 9.4x faster results (Query A: 123.3ms to 13.1ms)

claim: strict_order guarantees results ordered by exact distance while relaxed_order allows slightly out-of-order results for better recall; relaxed_order is the recommended default and strict_order is used when ranking precision matters, with partial indexes recommended for category-specific searches.
quote: Strict order guarantees that the returned results are ordered by exact distance. Relaxed order allows results that are slightly out of order, but provides better recall ... Relaxed_order should be used by default, while strict_order should be used when ranking precision matters.

claim: A concrete hybrid pattern adds a STORED generated tsvector column (to_tsvector('english', content)) with a GIN index alongside an HNSW vector index, runs both searches, and fuses by reciprocal rank fusion with score 1/(k+rank), k=60, over-fetching ~20 candidates per side to return top 10.
quote: ADD COLUMN search_vector tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', content)) STORED; CREATE INDEX idx_chunks_search ON document_chunks USING gin(search_vector); ... RRF_score(d) = Σ 1 / (k + rank_i(d)) where k=60

claim: Hybrid search merges a vector ANN list and a lexical (BM25/tsvector) list with reciprocal rank fusion using the standard k=60 smoothing constant, combining rankings rather than raw scores so disparate score distributions need not be normalized.
quote: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), which combines rankings rather than raw scores, with each result getting a score of 1 / (k + rank) where k is a smoothing constant (usually 60)

claim: DeepEye-SQL's Semantic Value Retrieval module extracts unique values from TEXT columns and embeds them so the LLM is supplied a relevant subset of real database values, preventing hallucinated or mismatched filter values (the grounding problem).
quote: DeepEye-SQL incorporates a Semantic Value Retrieval module that proactively supplies the LLM with a contextually relevant subset of database values. Instead of indexing every value, selective extraction is performed targeting columns of type TEXT as they are the primary source of ambiguity and value-related hallucinations.

claim: Vanna.AI (23,582 GitHub stars) is a RAG text-to-SQL framework that embeds DDL statements, business documentation, and example SQL queries into a vector store and retrieves the most relevant pieces by similarity to build the LLM prompt.
quote: Vanna works in two easy steps - train a RAG model on your data, and then ask questions... Whenever you ask a new question, Vanna will retrieve 10 most relevant pieces of training data and use it as part of the prompt to generate the SQL.

claim: Vanna stores embeddings of DDL, documentation, and SQL examples in a vector store and at query time retrieves the 10 most relevant pieces of training data via semantic matching to inject into the SQL-generation prompt.
quote: Whenever you ask a new question, Vanna will retrieve 10 most relevant pieces of training data and use it as part of the LLM prompt to generate the SQL.

claim: DAIL-SQL (635 GitHub stars) selects few-shot examples by joint question- and query-level similarity, masking domain-specific tokens then filtering candidates by query (SQL) similarity, achieving 86.6% execution accuracy on the Spider leaderboard with GPT-4.
quote: DAIL-SQL refreshes the Spider leaderboard with 86.6% execution accuracy and wins the first place... DAIL Selection retrieves examples by jointly considering question- and query-level similarity.

claim: LlamaIndex's PGVectorSQLQueryEngine teaches the LLM to emit SQL using pgvector's <-> nearest-neighbor operator with a [query_vector] placeholder, unifying semantic row retrieval (ORDER BY embedding <-> query) and structured WHERE filtering in a single SQL statement.
quote: We use specialized pgvector syntax (`<->`) to do nearest neighbors/semantic search to a given vector from an embeddings column... This allows you to do both semantic search and structured querying, _all_ within SQL.

claim: For large schemas, schema linking combines a retrieval module and column selector: top-k columns per query keyword are retrieved by embedding-based semantic similarity between keywords and column descriptions, so only relevant columns are passed to the SQL-generating LLM.
quote: Based on semantic similarity between keywords and column descriptions, the top-k columns for each keyword can be retrieved.

claim: On 50M Cohere 768-dim embeddings, Postgres with pgvector+pgvectorscale (StreamingDiskANN) achieved 28x lower p95 latency and 16x higher throughput than Pinecone s1 at 99% recall, at ~75% lower cost ($835 vs $3,241/mo).
quote: 28x lower p95 latency and 16x higher query throughput compared to Pinecone's storage optimized (s1) index for approximate nearest neighbor queries at 99% recall ... $835 ... $3,241

claim: pgvectorscale adds StreamingDiskANN (a disk-based index inspired by Microsoft DiskANN), Statistical Binary Quantization compression, and label-based filtered vector search via Microsoft Filtered DiskANN research.
quote: A new index type called StreamingDiskANN, inspired by the DiskANN algorithm ... Statistical Binary Quantization ... Label-based filtered vector search: based on Microsoft's Filtered DiskANN research

claim: Keeping vectors as a native Postgres column lets vector similarity combine with any SQL filter (WHERE, JOINs, full-text) and keeps relational and vector workloads transactionally consistent with full referential integrity, avoiding multi-system sync.
quote: your relational workload and vector workload are transactionally consistent with full referential integrity so you never get dangling records ... combine vector similarity search with any standard SQL filter: WHERE clauses, JOINs, full-text search

claim: 2026 throughput estimates: pgvector ~5K-15K QPS, Qdrant ~30K-80K QPS, Weaviate ~25K-50K QPS, Milvus 100K+ QPS at scale; guidance is pgvector if you have Postgres, Qdrant if not, Milvus only at very large scale.
quote: pgvector if you have Postgres, Qdrant if you do not. Reach for Milvus only at very large scale ... ~5K-15K QPS ... ~30K-80K QPS ... 100K+ QPS at scale

claim: For most SMB RAG under ~5M vectors pgvector is the correct default; reach for a dedicated store only at measurable limits, with Pinecone winning ease at 5M+, Qdrant fastest filtered search, Weaviate built-in hybrid search, Milvus at billion-vector scale.
quote: for most SMB RAG use cases under 5M vectors, pgvector is the correct default ... Pinecone wins at 5M+ vectors ... Qdrant if you need the absolute fastest filtered search ... Milvus if you're working at billion-vector scale

claim: At 100M-vector scale, monthly cost estimates put Qdrant on-disk HNSW at ~$600-900, Weaviate ~$700-1,000, Milvus ~$800-1,200, and Pinecone pods at $4,000-7,000+, making self-hosting economically justified at that scale.
quote: Qdrant self-hosted with on-disk HNSW (~$600-900/month ... Milvus on Kubernetes (~$800-1,200/month) ... Pinecone pods ($4,000-7,000+/month) ... Weaviate self-hosted cluster (~$700-1,000/month)

claim: GitHub stars (June 2026): pgvector/pgvector ~21.7K, timescale/pgvectorscale ~3.0K, qdrant/qdrant ~32.0K, weaviate/weaviate ~16.3K, milvus-io/milvus ~44.7K.
quote: Postgres extension for vector search (DiskANN), complements pgvector for performance and scale. Postgres OSS licensed.

claim: pgvector applies metadata filters AFTER the HNSW index returns its ef_search candidates (post-filtering), so a WHERE clause can leave far fewer rows than the LIMIT requested.
quote: Post-filtering misses some good green candidates that were ignored because some others where selected.

claim: On a partitioned table with ~40M rows per partition at 768 dims, HNSW index creation stalled at 29.2% after 19+ hours even with maintenance_work_mem=40GB and 11 parallel workers.
quote: hnsw graph no longer fits into maintenance_work_mem after 570905 tuples

claim: HNSW builds run 10-50x slower on the disk-based path when the graph exceeds maintenance_work_mem (default 64MB), and Postgres emits a notice when this happens.
quote: Indexes build significantly faster when the graph fits into maintenance_work_mem

claim: With the default hnsw.ef_search of 40, a filter matching only 10% of rows yields on average just 4 results, so LIMIT can silently return fewer rows than requested before iterative scans (added in 0.8.0).
quote: If a condition matches 10% of rows, with HNSW and the default hnsw.ef_search of 40, only 4 rows will match on average.

claim: pgvector's indexable vector type tops out at 2,000 dimensions (halfvec to 4,000, bit to 64,000), HNSW indexes do not reclaim space on row deletes causing bloat and recall drift, and native sharding of vector data across nodes is not supported.
quote: HNSW indexes do not reclaim space when rows are deleted ... Native sharding of vector data across nodes is not supported

claim: Filtered vector search latency can range from 50ms (pre-filter) to 5 seconds (post-filter), HNSW builds on a few million vectors can consume 10+GB RAM, and forcing overfetch (LIMIT 100 to get 10) gives no correctness guarantee.
quote: HNSW index creation on a few million vectors can consume 10+ GB of RAM or more

claim: A widely-discussed Hacker News thread 'The Case Against PGVector' debates pgvector's production tradeoffs around filtered search, scaling beyond cache, and OLTP resource contention.
quote: The Case Against PGVector

claim: pgvector is appropriate when the dataset fits one Postgres instance with moderate filter selectivity, but vector workloads share CPU/memory/IO with OLTP traffic and a burst of vector queries can starve transactional queries of buffer cache and parallel workers.
quote: a burst of vector queries can starve transactional queries of buffer cache and parallel workers

claim: Keeping embeddings fresh in pgvector is an operational burden: in-place batch re-embedding leaves the index in a partially-stale state, and the dominant cost is coordinating backfill and observability into which documents changed, not the API calls.
quote: Stale embeddings are a real RAG quality problem - when the vector store lags behind the source database, your retrieval quality degrades.

claim: The CHESS text-to-SQL framework's Information Retriever agent resolves natural-language keywords to actual database cell values using LSH plus vector-database semantic similarity, built in a preprocessing step that creates minhash, LSH, and vector indices per database.
quote: preprocessing creates the minhash, LSH, and vector databases for each of the databases in the specified directory ... converts raw database values into searchable indices that enable rapid semantic matching between natural language question keywords and actual database cell values

claim: A practitioner blog frames text-to-SQL 'value linking' as connecting a user's natural-language entity to the canonical stored DB value (e.g. 'online-only schools' to the stored 'F'), the problem that semantic search over a column's distinct values conventionally solves.
quote: value linking ... connecting user natural-language queries to actual database column values when they don't match directly. User says 'online-only schools' -> database stores 'F' in a Virtual column

claim: An independent practitioner benchmark on 1M OpenAI 1536-dim embeddings (ann-benchmarks framework, t3.2xlarge) found Qdrant outperformed pgvector's IVF index in throughput by ~15x with p95 latency of 2.85s worst-case vs pgvector's 4.02s best / 45.46s worst case.
quote: lagging behind Qdrant by a factor of 15 ... Qdrant worst case: 2.85 seconds; pgvector best case: 4.02 seconds; pgvector worst case: 45.46 seconds ... pgvector is ~18% less accurate ... pgvector: IVF-based indexing (lists=200, probes=2)

claim: An independent (non-database-vendor) comparison reports pgvector+pgvectorscale at 471 QPS @ 99% recall on 50M vectors versus Qdrant's 41.47 QPS (11.4x), corroborating that HNSW-based pgvector throughput numbers are scale- and index-dependent.
quote: pgvectorscale: 471 QPS at 99% recall on 50 million vectors; Qdrant: 41.47 QPS at 99% recall (11.4x slower) ... Firecrawl is not a vendor of any vector database listed
